area: Area VI. Flight by Reference to Instruments
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain what leads to unusual attitudes, teach nose-high and nose-low recoveries on a full panel, a partial panel and a glass panel's backup instruments, set up an unusual attitude safely with a positive exchange of controls, demonstrate a recovery under the hood while explaining it, and name, explain and fix a learner's interpretation and control errors.
why: This Task is on every CFII checkride: the Area VI NOTE in FAA-S-8081-9E says the evaluator shall select Task H. Loss of control in flight is the leading cause of fatal general aviation accidents [[24:106|AFH 5-1]], and instrument failure and continued VFR into IMC are named loss of control scenarios [[30:22|RMH 3-4]]. Without proper training in instrument interpretation and aircraft control, a pilot can quickly turn an abnormal attitude into a potentially fatal accident [[23:216|IFH 7-55]]. The recoveries you teach are what your instrument learner will have on the day a vacuum pump or an AHRS quits in cloud.

warmup: Think first: on your CFII checkride the examiner says "Eyes closed, head down, I have the flight controls," then hands you back an airplane with the airspeed climbing, the altimeter unwinding and the attitude indicator covered. Which instruments do you read first, what do you move first, and what are you saying out loud while you do it?

key_terms.def: An airplane attitude not normally required for instrument flight. Except in training it is not intentional, so it is often unexpected [[23:187|IFH 7-26]].

An event that unintentionally exceeds the parameters normally seen in flight or training: more than 25° nose up, more than 10° nose down, more than 45° of bank, or an airspeed inappropriate for the conditions [[24:106|AFH 5-1]].
Airspeed decreasing or below the desired airspeed, with the altimeter and VSI showing a climb; the attitude indicator shows it at once except in extreme attitudes [[23:188|IFH 7-27]].
The same instruments in the opposite direction: airspeed increasing or above the desired airspeed, altitude decreasing [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

Flight with the attitude gyro and heading indicator covered or inoperative on analog instruments, or with the AHRS simulated or rendered inoperative on an electronic display [[23:162|IFH 7-1]] [[23:194|IFH 7-33]].
An older type with pitch and roll limits, about 60° and 100°, beyond which the gyro tumbles; do not depend on it in an unusual attitude [[23:114|IFH 5-19]] [[23:188|IFH 7-27]].
PFD software, made possible by the AHRS, that shows red chevrons pointing back to the horizon and declutters the display in extreme pitch or bank [[23:216|IFH 7-55]] [[23:217|IFH 7-56]].

In the IFH example glass airplane, an analog airspeed indicator, attitude indicator, altimeter and magnetic compass for use when the PFD is unavailable, with no standby turn coordinator [[23:331|IFH 11-6]] [[23:219|IFH 7-58]].
The lack of orientation with regard to the position, attitude or movement of the airplane in space [[1:428|PHAK 17-6]].
A prolonged coordinated turn feels like no turn; the pilot sees the altitude loss, pulls back, and tightens the spiral [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].
The three-step "You have the flight controls", "I have the flight controls", "You have the flight controls" procedure, with a visual check [[25:178|AIH 9-8]] [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].
Instructor tells and does, learner tells while the instructor does, learner tells and does, then learner does while the instructor evaluates [[25:177|AIH 9-7]] [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

chunks.title: What this Task asks, and how it is tested

body.p: The Area VI NOTE in the CFII PTS (FAA-S-8081-9E) says the evaluator shall select Task H and at least one other Task, so plan on teaching this one on every checkride. The same NOTE lets you choose either the primary and supporting or the control and performance method for teaching the Area; pick one and keep its words all the way through. The PTS also has you use a view-limiting device for this Task.

**The words.** An unusual attitude is an airplane attitude not normally required for instrument flight. Except in training it is not intentional, so it is often unexpected, and the reaction of an inexperienced or inadequately trained pilot is usually instinctive rather than intelligent and deliberate [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]. With practice, the techniques for rapid and safe recovery can be mastered [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]. The AFH adds the word **upset**: it has defined limits, includes stalls and inappropriate airspeeds, and centers on surprise. An instructor-set 30° bank with the nose 15° up is an unusual attitude, not an upset [[24:106|AFH 5-1]] [[24:107|AFH 5-2]].
What the Task objective in the PTS asks for, element by element:

What the examiner listens and watches for

K1b Procedure

K2a, K2b Common errors

S1 Demonstrate and explain

body.p: **What the PTS adds for every Task.** The examiner will act as a student during selected maneuvers to test your analysis and correction of simulated common errors, but will not simulate any condition that may jeopardize safe flight or damage the airplane. Your explanation during a demonstration must be clear, concise, technically accurate and complete, with no prompting. Maneuvers that do not fit the scenario, unusual attitudes among them, may be flown after it (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction).

callout.text: The pilot's side of this Task is in the Instrument lesson IR.IV.B, and the CFI lesson AI.XI.E covers teaching unusual attitudes to VFR learners. This lesson adds what an instrument instructor needs: partial panel and glass backup recoveries, the setup and exchange of controls, a talk-through you can fly, and error analysis.

check.q: The examiner asks why this Task is on your test even though your scenario never needed it. What do you answer?
check.a: The Area VI NOTE requires the evaluator to select Task H on every test, and maneuvers such as unusual attitudes that do not fit the scenario may be flown after it (FAA-S-8081-9E).

chunks.title: Conditions that lead to unusual attitudes

body.p: **Conditions or situations which contribute to the development of unusual flight attitudes** (K1a). Teach the IFH list by name: turbulence, disorientation, instrument failure, confusion, preoccupation with flight deck duties, carelessness in cross-checking, errors in instrument interpretation, and lack of proficiency in aircraft control [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]. Each one is a habit or a hazard the learner can work on before meeting it in cloud.

head: Condition
How it builds
Prevention you teach
rows: Turbulence
A large variation in wind over a short distance, plus mountain waves, wind shear, thunderstorms and wake turbulence [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]
Brief the weather. In a thunderstorm, hold a level attitude and let airspeed and altitude vary [[23:327|IFH 11-2]]
Disorientation
False sensations take over once the eyes lose the horizon [[1:428|PHAK 17-6]]
Trust the instruments and disregard the sensations [[23:76|IFH 3-9]]
Instrument failure
Gyros slowing after a vacuum failure wander; a pilot who misses the off flags can turn a benign failure into a dangerous unusual attitude [[23:332|IFH 11-7]] [[23:333|IFH 11-8]]
Vacuum gauge and flags in the scan; practice without the attitude and heading indicators [[23:333|IFH 11-8]]
Confusion
The impulse to stop and stare at a discrepancy until trained for immediate recognition [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
Drill recognition on the ground with the IFH figures
Preoccupation with flight deck duties
Hunting for charts, logs or computers pulls attention off the instruments [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
Items for the flight neatly arranged for easy access [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]
Carelessness in cross-checking
A flight deck interruption while holding pressures can easily lead to an unusual attitude [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
Keep the airplane trimmed for level flight at all times [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]
Errors in instrument interpretation
Listed by the IFH as a cause [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]; the K2a chunk covers the forms it takes
Teach how each instrument works and fails [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]
Lack of proficiency in aircraft control
Skill levels diminish when basic attitude instrument flying is not practiced for long periods [[23:221|IFH 7-60]]
Avoid IMC when not proficient and get instruction first [[23:221|IFH 7-60]]

body.p: **The bigger picture.** The AFH groups upset causes as environmental, mechanical, human and stall-related factors [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]. Human factors include continued VFR into IMC, diversion of attention (even setting avionics while flying) and task saturation, such as a fatigued pilot at night in IMC with a vacuum pump failure facing extended, unpracticed partial panel flight [[24:107|AFH 5-2]] [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]. With instrument failures, avoiding an upset may depend on proficiency with secondary instruments and partial panel [[24:107|AFH 5-2]].

**Loss of situational awareness** comes from distractions, unexpected events, complacency, high workload, unfamiliar situations and inoperative equipment. A pneumatic failure that takes the attitude and heading indicators can leave a pilot in an unusual attitude [[23:337|IFH 11-12]].

callout.text: Application: group the eight IFH conditions in three: the air (turbulence), the panel (instrument failure, interpretation errors) and the pilot (disorientation, confusion, preoccupation, careless cross-check, weak control skills).

check.q: Your instrument learner says unusual attitudes only happen in turbulence. Which IFH conditions do you add, and why do they matter in a single-vacuum trainer?
check.a: Disorientation, instrument failure, confusion, preoccupation with flight deck duties, careless cross-checking, interpretation errors and weak control proficiency [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]. A vacuum failure the pilot does not notice can lead to a dangerous unusual attitude that needs a partial panel recovery [[23:333|IFH 11-8]].

chunks.title: Spatial disorientation, and how to let the learner feel it

body.p: Spatial disorientation is the lack of orientation with regard to the position, attitude or movement of the airplane in space. In VMC the eyes usually win over false sensations; take the visual cues away and false sensations can disorient a pilot quickly [[1:428|PHAK 17-6]]. The AFH counts nearly 200 spatial disorientation accidents from 2008 to 2013, more than 70% of them fatal, and warns that disoriented pilots may not know it [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]. The PTS asks the examiner to emphasize your ability to teach spatial disorientation (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction).

head: Illusion
Cause
The unusual attitude it leads to
rows: The leans
A bank entered too slowly to sense; a rotational acceleration of 2° per second or lower is below the detection threshold of the semicircular canals [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]]
Leveling feels like a bank the other way; the pilot rolls back into the original bank or leans [[23:72|IFH 3-5]]
Graveyard spiral
A prolonged coordinated turn feels like no turn, and the pilot notices altitude loss [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]
The pilot pulls back, which tightens the spiral and increases the altitude loss [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]
Coriolis
A head movement in a different plane during a prolonged turn [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]
Illusion of turning on a different axis; the pilot may maneuver into a dangerous attitude [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]
Somatogravic
Rapid acceleration feels nose-up; rapid deceleration feels nose-down [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]
A push into a nose-low or dive attitude, or a pull into a nose-up or stall attitude [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]
Inversion
An abrupt change from climb to straight-and-level flight [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]
An abrupt push into a nose-low attitude [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]
Elevator
An abrupt updraft or downdraft [[23:73|IFH 3-6]] [[23:74|IFH 3-7]]
Updraft: a push nose-low; downdraft: a pull nose-up [[23:74|IFH 3-7]]

body.p: **Let the learner feel it.** The IFH gives instructor-flown demonstrations with the learner's eyes closed: accelerating in level flight feels like a climb, and a slowly entered, coordinated turn of about 50° also feels like a climb [[23:75|IFH 3-8]]. Even no sensation is a result, because it shows the body cannot detect bank or roll [[23:74|IFH 3-7]]. A learner-flown version works too: eyes closed and head tilted, the learner follows your control instructions until disoriented, then you say to look up and recover [[23:75|IFH 3-8]]. The goal is more confidence in the flight instruments [[23:74|IFH 3-7]].

callout.text: Never fly these demonstrations at low altitudes or without an instructor or appropriate safety pilot [[23:75|IFH 3-8]]. Rolling beyond the vertical plane usually produces an intense disorientation [[23:75|IFH 3-8]], so save it for after the gentle ones. Application: debrief each one in one line: "What did you feel, and what did the panel show?"

check.q: Your learner felt nothing at all during your slow 50° coordinated turn with her eyes closed. Was the demonstration wasted?
check.a: No. Any false sensation is an effective demonstration, and the absence of sensation still shows that the body cannot detect bank or roll [[23:74|IFH 3-7]].

chunks.title: Recognize and assess before you move

body.p: Every recovery starts with recognition. As a general rule, any time an instrument rate of movement or indication is not one of those of the basic maneuvers, assume an unusual attitude and speed up the cross-check to confirm the attitude, an instrument error or an instrument malfunction [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]. The immediate problem is not how the airplane got there, but what it is doing and how to get back to straight-and-level as quickly as possible [[23:188|IFH 7-27]].

head: Instrument
Nose-high
Nose-low
rows: Airspeed
Decreasing, or below the desired airspeed [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]
Increasing, or above the desired airspeed [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
Altimeter
Gaining altitude [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]
Losing altitude [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
VSI
Descent, the opposite direction [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]
Attitude indicator
Nose up, at a glance, except in extreme attitudes [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]
Nose down, with the same limits [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]
Turn coordinator and ball
Direction of turn; unless the ball is centered, do not assume the turn comes from a bank [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]

body.p: **Teach the order of reading.** Airspeed gives the pitch direction and so picks the recovery: decreasing means the nose-high recovery, increasing means the nose-low one [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. The attitude indicator and turn coordinator give the bank, and the ball shows coordination [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. Application: have the learner say it in that order, "Airspeed decreasing, altimeter climbing, right turn: nose-high."

**On a PFD** the trend vectors show where airspeed and altitude will be in 6 seconds, the heading trend shows which way the airplane is turning, and the slip/skid indicator shows coordination; together they help the pilot tell which type of unusual attitude it is [[23:217|IFH 7-56]].

callout.text: Incorrect assessment of what kind of upset the airplane is in heads the AFH list of recovery errors [[24:112|AFH 5-7]]. A learner who moves the yoke before reading the airspeed has skipped the step that prevents it.

check.q: Under the hood your learner sees the airspeed rising past cruise, the altimeter unwinding and the turn coordinator showing a left turn. What should he call, and which recovery is it?
check.a: "Nose-low, left turn." Airspeed increasing and altitude decreasing are the nose-low picture, so he flies the nose-low recovery [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

chunks.title: Nose-high recovery, full panel and partial panel

body.p: **Procedure using full panel and partial panel for recovery from nose-high attitudes** (K1b). As soon as the unusual attitude is detected, start the recovery procedure in the POH/AFM. If there is none, start the recovery by reference to the airspeed indicator, altimeter, VSI and turn coordinator [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]. That is why the IFH recovery works with or without the attitude indicator.

**Full panel.** In moderate unusual attitudes the pilot can normally reorient by establishing a level flight indication on the attitude indicator. Do not depend on it if it is the spillable type, because its limits may have been exceeded or it may have failed; even a working nonspillable type can be off by up to 5° in pitch and bank and is very hard to read in extreme attitudes [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]. Application: on a full panel, a working nonspillable attitude indicator speeds up the recovery, and the other instruments confirm it.

head: IFH step
Full panel cue
Partial panel cue
rows: 1. Increase power as necessary, in proportion to the observed deceleration [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]
Airspeed loss slows
Airspeed loss slows
2. Forward elevator pressure to lower the nose and prevent a stall [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]
Miniature aircraft moves toward a level flight indication [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]
Airspeed and altimeter needles reverse and stabilize: level pitch [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
3. Coordinated aileron and rudder to level the miniature aircraft and center the ball of the turn coordinator [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]
Wings level on the attitude indicator, checked on the turn coordinator
Turn coordinator miniature aircraft level and ball centered: straight, coordinated flight [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
4. Stabilize, then return to the altitude assigned by the instructor or ATC [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
Normal cross-check
Altimeter primary for pitch once level, with small inputs [[23:197|IFH 7-36]]; VSI primary while returning [[23:198|IFH 7-37]]

body.p: The corrective inputs are made almost simultaneously, but in that order [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]. Why power first: the airspeed is decreasing, so power goes in, in proportion to the deceleration, and forward pressure lowers the nose to prevent a stall [[23:188|IFH 7-27]].

**When it is already a stall.** If the stall warning or buffet is there, fly the stall recovery instead: reduce the angle of attack first, then roll wings level, then add power as needed. Power reduces the altitude loss but does not end a stall, and the return to the flightpath must be smooth to avoid a secondary stall [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. The IFH says the same for stall practice: respond to a stall warning or aerodynamic indication by smoothly reducing the angle of attack and applying maximum power, or as the POH/AFM recommends [[23:187|IFH 7-26]].

callout.text: Application: say the partial panel cue out loud when you demonstrate: "Altimeter stopped, airspeed stopped, that's level pitch." With the gyros covered, those two needles reversing and holding steady is the learner's level pitch picture [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

check.q: Partial panel, nose-high, airspeed falling. Your learner adds power and lowers the nose. Without an attitude indicator, how does he know the pitch is level?
check.a: A level pitch attitude is shown by the reversal and stabilization of the airspeed and altimeter needles [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

chunks.title: Nose-low recovery and the spiral dive

body.p: **Procedure for recovery from nose-low attitudes** (K1b). If the airspeed is increasing or above the desired airspeed, the IFH order is [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]:

bullets: 1. **Power:** reduce power to prevent excessive airspeed and loss of altitude [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

2. **Bank:** correct to straight flight with coordinated aileron and rudder by referring to the turn coordinator. Keep the ball centered: slipping and skidding sensations can aggravate disorientation and slow the recovery [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].
3. **Pitch:** raise the nose to level flight with smooth back elevator pressure [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

4. **Watch for overcontrol:** the first control pressures may be large, so keep a fast cross-check. Needles slowing means approaching level; needles stopping and reversing means passing through level [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].
5. **Add the attitude indicator** to the cross-check once the airspeed, altimeter and turn coordinator stabilize, then return to the assigned altitude [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

body.p: **By the numbers first.** In a smooth, proficient recovery all controls change at once, but in initial training the IFH wants a positive, confident recovery by the numbers, in that order [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. The instinctive reaction to a nose-down attitude is to pull back on the elevator control [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. In a banked descent that pull tightens the spiral [[23:73|IFH 3-6]], so teach the learner to level the wings before raising the nose.

**Full panel or partial panel.** With a working attitude indicator, check it and the turn coordinator for the bank [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. On partial panel the turn coordinator and ball give the bank, and level pitch shows as the airspeed and altimeter needles stop and reverse [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. The turn coordinator shows only rate and direction of turn, not an angle of bank [[1:219|PHAK 8-17]].

**The spiral dive** is a nose-low upset in which airspeed and G-load can rise rapidly. In IMC the sound of increasing speed may be the first clue, and a startled pilot who pulls back while rolling level can cause structural damage or failure [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. The AFH gives five steps:

head: Step
AFH spiral dive recovery
rows: Power to idle, to slow the acceleration [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]
Some forward elevator to about +1 G ("unload"), so the spiral is not aggravated and a rolling pullout is prevented [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]
Roll wings level with coordinated aileron and rudder, all the way level before step 4 [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]
Gently raise the nose to level flight; the speed may be at or beyond VNE [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]
Climb power once the airspeed has stabilized at VY, and climb back to a safe altitude [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]

body.p: **Why gentle matters.** In a level, coordinated turn the load factor is 2 G at 60° of bank, and the normal category limit load factor is 3.8 [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]. Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor, so an airplane that stalls at 50 knots can stall at 100 knots at 4 G [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]] [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]]. Flying at or below VA does not protect against full inputs in more than one axis at the same time [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].

callout.text: Nose-high: power up, push, roll. Nose-low: power down, roll, then a smooth pull.

check.q: Nose-low, 50° of left bank, airspeed rising fast. Your learner pulls back first. What does the pull do, and what is the fix?
check.a: Pulling in a steep descending turn tightens the spiral [[23:73|IFH 3-6]], and pulling while rolling level can overstress the airframe [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. Fix: power off, level the wings with coordinated aileron and rudder, then smooth back pressure [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

body.p: The PTS puts special emphasis on partial panel because of fatal accidents involving spatial disorientation of instrument-rated pilots who flew in clouds with inoperative gyro instruments, and because many light airplanes in IMC have only a single vacuum source (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction). In the IFH, every analog maneuver except the instrument takeoff can be flown partial panel, with the attitude gyro and heading indicator covered or inoperative [[23:162|IFH 7-1]].

**Spot the failure first.** A warning indicator, or an attitude indicator that disagrees with the supporting performance instruments, usually identifies a failure. Expedite the cross-check, compare the attitude indicator at once with the rate-of-turn indicator and VSI, then use the instruments that still work; covering the failed ones may help [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]. In Figure 11-8 the airplane is actually level at 2,000 feet, not turning left [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]. Many small airplanes have no vacuum warning, so the vacuum gauge belongs in the scan [[23:332|IFH 11-7]] [[23:333|IFH 11-8]].

**The partial panel recovery** is the same IFH sequence: pitch from the airspeed indicator, altimeter and VSI, bank from the turn coordinator and ball [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. Once level, the altimeter is the primary pitch reference. First make a smooth input to stop the needle, then change pitch to go back; abrupt yoke inputs give large pitch changes and swing the airplane from nose-high to nose-low and back [[23:197|IFH 7-36]]. For the return, use a vertical speed about double the altitude error, never more than the airplane's optimum rate, which varies from 500 to 1,000 fpm [[23:197|IFH 7-36]] [[23:198|IFH 7-37]].

**Turn needle airplanes.** A footnote in Area VI of the PTS says that if the test airplane has a turn needle, substitute the turn needle for the miniature aircraft of the turn coordinator. Teach the difference: the turn-and-slip indicator's gyro senses yaw, while the turn coordinator's canted gyro senses roll and yaw, so it first shows the rate of roll and then the rate of turn [[23:116|IFH 5-21]].

callout.text: Application: cover the attitude and heading indicators while the learner's eyes are closed, so the first look at the panel is the failure picture. It trains the habit the IFH asks for: practicing instrument flight without the attitude and heading indicators in preparation for a vacuum failure [[23:333|IFH 11-8]].

check.q: The attitude indicator shows a steady left bank, but the turn coordinator is level and the VSI reads zero. What do you teach your learner to conclude and do?
check.a: An inconsistency between the attitude indicator and the performance instruments usually means a failure. Compare it with the turn coordinator and VSI, fly by the instruments that work, cover the failed one, then advise ATC [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].

chunks.title: Glass panels: protection, AHRS failure and backup instruments

body.p: The PTS asks you to teach the Area VI Tasks with the full panel and with reference to backup flight instruments or electronic displays, and notes that backup instruments in technically advanced airplanes may not sit directly in front of the pilot (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction). On an electronic flight display, every maneuver except the instrument takeoff can be flown partial panel with the AHRS simulated or rendered inoperative [[23:194|IFH 7-33]].

head: Feature (IFH example display)
What the learner should know
rows: Full-width horizon

Keeps some sky and some ground in view at all times, so the pilot always knows the quickest way back to the horizon. The horizon line starts moving down at about 47° nose-up and up at about 27° nose-down [[23:216|IFH 7-55]]
White line and blue-brown break
The white line is the horizon; the break between blue and brown is only a reference [[23:216|IFH 7-55]]
Red chevrons, nose-high
Appear approaching 30° nose-up and point back to the horizon; the display declutters, and the rest returns below 25° [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]
Red chevrons, nose-low
Appear past 15° nose-down; the display declutters at 20° nose-down [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]
Bank past 60°
The roll index extends to show the shortest way back to wings level; the display declutters at 65° [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]
Trend vectors
Airspeed and altitude 6 seconds ahead; the heading trend shows which way the airplane is turning [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]

body.p: **AHRS failure.** All unusual attitude protection is lost, along with all attitude and heading indications on the PFD and every autopilot mode except roll and altitude hold [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]. In Figure 7-73 the altimeter and VSI tape are the only clear signs of the nose-high attitude, the slip/skid indicator is gone, no standby turn coordinator is installed, and the magnetic compass is less useful than a turn coordinator [[23:217|IFH 7-56]].

**AHRS and air data both failed.** Only the standby airspeed indicator, attitude indicator, altimeter and magnetic compass are left, with no standby turn coordinator, and in extreme pitch or bank the analog standby attitude indicator may tumble [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]. The manufacturer of the IFH example airplane recommends turning on the autopilot, whose roll mode is a wing leveler fed by its own turn coordinator behind the MFD [[23:219|IFH 7-58]].

callout.text: Pilots should consult the POH/AFM for the power source of every instrument [[23:114|IFH 5-19]]. Application: the chevron and declutter numbers above come from the display in the IFH figures. Have the learner find the same items, and where the standby instruments sit, in the AFM or supplement for their own avionics, and agree before flight how you will simulate an AHRS failure.

check.q: You simulate an AHRS failure on a glass trainer with the airplane nose-high. On the PFD, what still shows the attitude, and what is missing?
check.a: The altimeter and VSI tape are the only clear signs of the nose-high attitude; the slip/skid indicator is gone, there is no standby turn coordinator, and all unusual attitude protection is lost [[23:217|IFH 7-56]].

chunks.title: Setting up an unusual attitude safely

body.p: **Where it fits.** The IFH sample lesson guide puts a spatial disorientation demonstration in Lesson 3, partial panel operations in Lesson 6, and recovery from unusual attitudes with partial panel practice in Lesson 7 [[23:342|IFH B-1]] [[23:343|IFH B-2]]. You put the airplane into a strange attitude on purpose, with a learner who cannot see out, so plan the setup like any maneuver with a safety brief.

head: Item
What to do
rows: Brief on the ground

Objectives, the steps, the expected result and the safety procedures [[25:175|AIH 9-5]], including how the controls will be exchanged [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. For an anxious learner, describe the sensations to expect and treat fear as a normal reaction [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]
Safety pilot and weather

Simulated instrument flight needs a safety pilot in the other control seat with at least a private certificate for the category and class [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]] and adequate vision forward and to each side [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(2)]]. The weather must make up for the safety pilot's restricted view, with more margin near busy airways or airports [[33:258|AIM 4-3-16]]
Area and altitude

Clear the area at and below your altitude and make sure there is enough altitude for a recovery [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. The IFH setup for stall practice fits: safe altitude above the terrain, no conflicting traffic, suitable weather and radar traffic advisories [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]
Size of the attitude

Stay inside the maneuvers approved for the airplane [[24:112|AFH 5-7]]. The AFH training example is 30° of bank with the nose 15° up [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]. With a non-crewmember aboard, intentional maneuvers past 60° of bank or 30° of pitch need parachutes for all, except on flight tests and for required maneuvers given by a CFI [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(c)]] [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(d)]]
Night
Practice unusual attitude recoveries at night only with a flight instructor [[24:224|AFH 11-7]]

body.p: **The setup, step by step.** No source gives a script for this Task, so the steps below are built from related sources and marked as application. In unusual attitude training the pilot is often told to close their eyes [[24:107|AFH 5-2]], and the disorientation demonstrations use eyes closed or the gaze lowered to the floor [[23:75|IFH 3-8]].

bullets: 1. Take the airplane with the three-step exchange: the learner says "You have the flight controls," you answer "I have the flight controls," the learner says it again, and you check visually [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].
2. Application: "Eyes closed, head down, hands in your lap, feet flat on the floor." Clear the area again; your eyes stay outside.

3. Application: maneuver with slow, coordinated changes, for example a climbing turn one way, then a descending turn the other way, so the learner cannot follow the attitude by feel. A slowly established, coordinated turn produces the same feeling as a climb [[23:75|IFH 3-8]].

4. Application: stop in the training attitude, inside your limits, and say "Open your eyes and recover. You have the flight controls," then complete the exchange [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. The IFH ends its learner-flown demonstration the same way, telling the pilot to look up and recover [[23:75|IFH 3-8]].
5. Guard the controls and be ready to take them back, calmly announcing "I have the flight controls" [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

callout.text: Your eyes belong outside while the learner's head is down. See and avoid applies under IFR and VFR whenever the weather permits [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]], and the PTS lists failure to clear the area before and while performing maneuvers as a reason for an unsatisfactory test (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction).

check.q: Why does the AFH say eyes-closed unusual attitude training is not the same as a real upset, and what do you add later in training?
check.a: With the eyes closed, any element of surprise disappears [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]. Later, use scenario-based training with realistic distractions to provoke startle or surprise [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

body.p: There must always be a clear understanding of who has control of the airplane. The PTS strongly recommends a positive three-step exchange, briefed before flight and followed by a visual check, and lists positive exchange of the flight controls as a special emphasis area (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction). The AIH explains why: numerous accidents have come from confusion about who had control, particularly between learners and flight instructors [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

bullets: **Giving control:** "You have the flight controls." The learner answers at once, "I have the flight controls." You repeat, "You have the flight controls" [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].
**Taking it back:** the learner uses the same three steps and stays on the controls, flying, until you say "I have the flight controls" [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].
**Visual check:** look to see that the other person actually has the controls. There should never be any doubt about who is flying [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

**When you must take over:** take the controls and calmly announce "I have the flight controls." Anxious learners can be incredibly strong, and nothing is gained by fighting for control [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

body.p: **Two exchanges per setup.** In this Task the controls change hands twice: before the setup and at "recover," and the second one happens with the airplane already in an unusual attitude. Application: brief that the learner answers "I have the flight controls" and starts the recovery right away, and keep your hand near the yoke until the first inputs look right.

**Your limits.** With potentially hazardous maneuvers, be alert and ready to take control at any time, especially on a learner's first attempt [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Learners should never be allowed to exceed your limits, and you should not exceed your own ability to perceive a problem, decide and react [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

check.q: At "recover" your learner grabs the yoke and pulls without saying a word. What is the problem, and what do you do?
check.a: The exchange was not completed, so there is doubt about who is flying. Take the controls calmly with "I have the flight controls" [[25:179|AIH 9-9]], recover, and rebrief the three steps before the next setup.

body.p: S1 asks you to demonstrate and simultaneously explain a recovery solely by reference to instruments, and the PTS has you under a view-limiting device for it. This is the first step of the telling-and-doing technique: explain the power settings, attitudes and other pertinent factors while you fly, in the same sequence you briefed, and if the demonstration strays from the explanation, say so at once [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].
**A nose-high talk-through, full panel.** The examiner sets it up; you open your eyes on "recover":

head: You do
You say
rows: Take the controls with the exchange [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]
"I have the flight controls."
Speed up the cross-check [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]
"Airspeed decreasing, altimeter and VSI climbing, right bank on the attitude indicator and turn coordinator. Nose-high."
Power up in proportion to the deceleration [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]
"Power first, in proportion to how fast the airspeed is dropping."
Forward pressure to lower the nose [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]
"Nose down toward a level indication, to stop the airspeed loss and prevent a stall."
Coordinated aileron and rudder [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]
"Roll the wings level, ball centered."
Confirm level and straight [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
"Airspeed and altimeter reversed and steady: level. Turn coordinator level, ball centered: straight."
Return to the assigned altitude [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
"Now back to our assigned altitude at a normal rate."

body.p: **A nose-low talk-through, partial panel:** "Airspeed increasing, altimeter unwinding, left turn on the turn coordinator: nose-low. Power back. Roll level on the turn coordinator, ball centered. Now smooth back pressure. Needles slowing, we're nearing level. Airspeed and altimeter stopped: level. Watch for the overshoot. Once it's stable, back to altitude." Each line follows the IFH order and cues [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

**Then hand it over.** Next the learner tells while you fly, so you can check understanding before the learner has to manage the airplane; then the learner tells and does [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Thinking aloud during practice shows you whether an error comes from a misconception or from a lack of motor skill [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

callout.text: Application: on the checkride, explain to the examiner as if to a learner at the stage where you would teach this, in short sentences. The PTS wants the explanation clear, concise, technically accurate and complete, with no prompting (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction).

check.q: In your demonstration you roll level a moment before the nose comes down, not in the order you briefed. What does the AIH say to do?
check.a: If the demonstration does not closely conform to the explanation, acknowledge and explain the deviation immediately [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

chunks.title: Common error: incorrect interpretation of the flight instruments

body.p: **Incorrect interpretation of the flight instruments** (K2a) is an error of reading, not of the hands. Interpretation starts with each instrument's construction and operating principles, applied to the airplane, the maneuver and the conditions [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]. In AIH terms most of these are mistakes, errors of thought from gaps or misconceptions, rather than slips, which are errors of action [[25:84|AIH 3-33]].

head: What you see
Usual cause
Fix, and how you teach it
rows: Pushes forward although the airspeed is already high and rising
Misread the attitude: an incorrect assessment of the upset [[24:112|AFH 5-7]]
Name the attitude from airspeed before any input [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]; ground drill with Figures 7-39 and 7-40
Stops and stares at one odd needle; no input for several seconds
Slow cross-check and fixation, the impulse to stop and stare at a discrepancy [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
Cross-check several instruments for corroboration, not one [[23:221|IFH 7-60]]; point out fixation when it occurs [[25:83|AIH 3-32]]
Levels the wings on a flagged attitude indicator, or trusts a gyro past its limits
Missed the off flags [[23:332|IFH 11-7]] or forgot that a spillable gyro may have tumbled [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]
Compare the attitude indicator with the turn coordinator and VSI at once [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]; teach the limits of the installed gyro [[1:221|PHAK 8-19]]
Rolls the wrong way; the bank gets steeper
Read bank direction from a bank scale that moves opposite to the bank on some models [[1:221|PHAK 8-19]]
Bank direction from the miniature aircraft against the horizon bar [[1:221|PHAK 8-19]]; on a PFD, follow the extended roll index [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]
Treats the turn coordinator as a bank angle, or ignores the ball
The turn coordinator shows rate and direction of turn only [[1:219|PHAK 8-17]]; unless the ball is centered, the turn may not come from a bank [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]
Read the ball with the turn coordinator every time
On a PFD, levels the blue-brown break instead of the white line
Takes the color break for the horizon [[23:216|IFH 7-55]]
The white line is the horizon [[23:216|IFH 7-55]]
Recovers toward what the body says
Attempting to recover by sensations other than sight [[23:190|IFH 7-29]]; recovery by instinct almost always gives wrong corrections [[23:221|IFH 7-60]]
Disorientation demonstrations, then "trust the instruments" [[23:76|IFH 3-9]]

body.p: **Teach it on the ground first.** Show the IFH unusual attitude figures and the PFD pictures and have the learner call the attitude out loud, instrument by instrument. Correcting a misunderstanding before the learner is absorbed in flying the airplane is the point of the "learner tells" step [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Basic skills matter too: every basic instrument error is aggravated during unusual attitude recoveries until the elementary skills are mastered [[23:190|IFH 7-29]].

check.q: Your learner rolls right when the airplane is banked right, saying the pointer at the top of the attitude indicator was on the left. What do you teach?
check.a: On some models the bank scale moves opposite to the bank. Use the scale only for the amount of bank, and the miniature aircraft against the horizon bar for its direction [[1:221|PHAK 8-19]].

chunks.title: Common error: inappropriate application of controls

body.p: **Inappropriate application of controls** (K2b) is the error of the hands and feet. Its root is the untrained reaction: abrupt muscular effort that is purposeless and even hazardous in turbulence, at excessive speeds or at low altitudes [[23:187|IFH 7-26]] [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]. The AFH answer is proportional counter-response: control and power inputs in direct proportion to the amount and rate of change of roll, yaw, pitch or airspeed, so the airplane is not overstressed, unless ground contact is imminent [[24:109|AFH 5-4]] [[24:111|AFH 5-6]].

head: What you see
Usual cause
Fix
rows: Pulls back in a nose-low bank
The instinctive reaction to a nose-down attitude [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
Power, bank, then pitch [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]; in a steep spiral, unload before rolling [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]
Pulls while rolling level in a spiral
Startle [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]
Finish the roll before raising the nose; it is a listed spiral recovery error [[24:132|AFH 5-27]]
Adds power in a nose-low attitude, or none in a nose-high one
Mismanaged airspeed [[24:112|AFH 5-7]] [[24:132|AFH 5-27]]
Power is step one in both IFH sequences, in opposite directions [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
Shoves the nose well below level in a nose-high recovery
Too much forward pressure; it is only needed to lower the nose and prevent a stall [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]
Stop when the airspeed and altimeter needles reverse and stabilize [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
Nose-low turns into nose-high after the pull
Large first pressures without a fast cross-check [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
Ease off as the needles slow; stop as they stop [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
Ball well out of center during the roll
Aileron without rudder; slips and skids aggravate disorientation and slow the recovery [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
Coordinated aileron and rudder; "step on the ball" [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]]
Fights the controls with the wing leveler or autopilot on
Failure to disconnect [[24:112|AFH 5-7]]
Disconnect first when equipped [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]
Abrupt yoke movements on partial panel; altitude oscillates
Reacting abruptly to altitude changes [[23:197|IFH 7-36]]
Stop the needle with a smooth input, then change pitch to return [[23:197|IFH 7-36]]
Holds pressure, and the attitude wanders during a task
The airplane is not trimmed [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
Trim for level flight at all times [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]

body.p: **How you teach the control side.** Application: when it helps, show an error's result at a safe altitude, then the correct input, so the learner sees cause and effect. The AIH gives the instructor actions: explain that errors happen at every skill level, let the learner practice recovering from common errors, and point out errors when they occur and ask the learner to explain why [[25:86|AIH 3-35]].

callout.text: Read, name, then move: airspeed tells the direction, the turn coordinator tells the bank, and only then do the hands and feet move, in proportion.

check.q: In a nose-high recovery your learner pushes until the airspeed is far above cruise. Which error is this and what is the fix?
check.a: Inappropriate application of controls: too much forward pressure, which turns nose-high into nose-low. The push only needs to lower the nose and prevent a stall; level pitch shows when the airspeed and altimeter needles reverse and stabilize [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

body.p: For S2 the examiner flies as your learner and makes errors on purpose, but never one that jeopardizes safe flight (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction). Your job, out loud, has three parts: name the error, explain the cause, give the fix. That matches the AIH: point out errors when they occur and ask the learner why they happened [[25:86|AIH 3-35]].

head: The examiner, as learner
You: name and cause
You: fix
rows: Sees the airspeed rising and pulls first, in 45° of bank
"Inappropriate application of controls. You pulled before leveling the wings, the instinctive reaction to a nose-low attitude [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]."
"Power back, roll level on the turn coordinator, then smooth back pressure."
Adds power with the airspeed rising
"Power the wrong way, an airspeed management error [[24:112|AFH 5-7]]. Rising airspeed means nose-low, so power comes back, not up [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. Did you read it as nose-high?"
"Say the airspeed trend before you touch the throttle."
On partial panel, keeps pulling after the needles reverse
"Overcontrolling. When the needles stopped and reversed, you passed through level [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]."
"Ease off as the needles slow, and stop when they stop."
Levels the wings on a flagged attitude indicator
"Interpretation error. A flag or a disagreement with the turn coordinator and VSI means a failure [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]."
"Cover it and fly the turn coordinator and the pitch instruments."
Rolls level with aileron only, ball far out
"Uncoordinated. Slips and skids aggravate disorientation and slow the recovery [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]."
"Rudder with the aileron: step on the ball."
Stares at the altimeter and makes no input
"Fixation: stopping to stare at a discrepancy [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]."
"Keep the scan moving: airspeed, altimeter, turn coordinator."
Recovers well, then stays 300 feet below the assigned altitude
"The recovery isn't finished. Return to the assigned altitude once stable [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]."
"About 600 fpm: double the error, within the airplane's optimum rate [[23:197|IFH 7-36]] [[23:198|IFH 7-37]]."

body.p: **Fix the habit, not just the event.** Faulty habits are difficult to correct and need to be addressed as soon as possible [[25:126|AIH 5-23]]. When you see a deficiency, reteach: demonstrate, let the learner practice under direction, then evaluate the performance [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. In the debrief, use collaborative assessment: the learner's self-assessment first, then yours [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].

callout.text: Analyze before you correct, but never at the cost of safety. With potentially hazardous maneuvers, be ready to take control at any time [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. An action that needs the evaluator to step in to keep the flight safe is a listed reason for an unsatisfactory test (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction).

check.q: The examiner, as learner, recovers from a nose-low attitude and stays 300 feet low. What do you say?
check.a: Name it: the recovery is not finished; return to the assigned altitude after stabilizing [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. Fix: climb at about double the error, 600 fpm, within the airplane's optimum rate [[23:197|IFH 7-36]] [[23:198|IFH 7-37]].

scenario.title: First partial panel recoveries in a single-vacuum trainer
scenario.setup: You are a new CFII. Your instrument learner, Sam, has about 20 hours toward the rating in a fixed-pitch trainer with a six-pack panel and a single vacuum pump. Today's lesson is unusual attitude recoveries, full panel first, then with the attitude and heading indicators covered. The practice area lies beside a busy approach corridor, with haze below a broken layer. Next month Sam moves to the school's PFD trainer with standby instruments.

questions.q: On the ground, what goes into your briefing before the first setup?
questions.a: The objectives, the steps, the expected result and the safety procedures [[25:175|AIH 9-5]], including the exchange of flight controls [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Tell Sam what sensations to expect and treat any fear as normal [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].

questions.q: Where and how high do you fly it, with the haze and the corridor?
questions.a: Clear the area at and below you and keep enough altitude for a recovery [[24:121|AFH 5-16]], and borrow the IFH stall practice setup: a safe altitude, no conflicting traffic, suitable weather and radar traffic advisories [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]. The weather must make up for your restricted view as safety pilot, with more margin near busy airways [[33:258|AIM 4-3-16]], so moving away from the corridor is wise.

questions.q: Full panel, nose-low with 45° of left bank. Sam pulls back hard first. What do you say?
questions.a: Name it: inappropriate application of controls, the instinctive pull in a nose-low attitude [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. Cause: he moved before dealing with the bank. Fix: power back, roll level with coordinated aileron and rudder, then smooth back pressure [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. In a steep spiral, a pull while rolling can overstress the airframe [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

questions.q: With the gyros covered, Sam says he cannot tell when the nose is level. What do you teach?
questions.a: Level pitch is when the airspeed and altimeter needles stop and reverse, then stabilize; the turn coordinator and centered ball show straight, coordinated flight [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. After that the altimeter is the primary pitch reference, with small, smooth inputs [[23:197|IFH 7-36]].

questions.q: In the PFD trainer next month, what do you add to the lesson?
questions.a: The protection: the horizon always keeps some sky and ground, the white line is the horizon, red chevrons point back to level, and past 60° the roll index shows the shortest way to wings level [[23:216|IFH 7-55]] [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]. Then a simulated AHRS failure: the protection is gone, the altimeter and VSI tape show pitch, and there is no standby turn coordinator [[23:217|IFH 7-56]] [[23:219|IFH 7-58]].

questions.q: In the debrief Sam says he has it now. What do you tell him about keeping the skill?
questions.a: Upset recovery skills are perishable and need continuous reinforcement [[24:110|AFH 5-5]]. Skill levels diminish when basic attitude instrument flying is not practiced, and pilots should avoid IMC when they are not proficient [[23:221|IFH 7-60]].

skills.do: Under the view-limiting device, take the airplane from the examiner with a positive exchange, call the attitude from the instruments, and fly the IFH nose-high or nose-low recovery on a full panel, a partial panel or the glass standby instruments, explaining each input and cue as you make it.
skills.practice: Fly the talk-through aloud with another applicant as safety pilot [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]], explaining in the same order you fly it [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Say both IFH sequences from memory on the ground first [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

skills.do: While the examiner flies as your learner, spot each error, name it as incorrect interpretation or inappropriate application of controls, explain the cause and give the fix, and take the controls if safety needs it.
skills.practice: Take turns flying the errors in the K2a and K2b tables for each other from the right seat, and debrief each one with name, cause and fix [[25:86|AIH 3-35]].

quiz.q: The examiner, acting as your learner, sees a needle moving at a rate that does not fit the maneuver being flown. What is the IFH general rule for that moment?
options: Assume an unusual attitude and speed up the cross-check
Wait for the attitude indicator to settle before moving
Push forward at once, since most upsets are nose-high
Look outside for a horizon before trusting the panel
quiz.why: Any time an instrument rate or indication is not one of those of the basic maneuvers, assume an unusual attitude and increase the speed of the cross-check to confirm the attitude, an instrument error or a malfunction [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]. Pushing first skips assessment, the top AFH recovery error [[24:112|AFH 5-7]].

quiz.q: If the POH/AFM gives no unusual attitude recovery procedure, by reference to which instruments does the IFH say to start the recovery?
options: Attitude indicator, heading indicator, altimeter and VSI
Airspeed indicator, altimeter, VSI and turn coordinator
Attitude indicator and turn coordinator, then the compass
Altimeter, heading indicator, magnetic compass and VSI
quiz.why: With no POH/AFM procedure, start the recovery by reference to the airspeed indicator, altimeter, VSI and turn coordinator [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]. The attitude and heading indicators are the ones a vacuum failure can take away [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].

quiz.q: Your learner is nose-high with the airspeed falling fast. In the IFH sequence, what comes first?
options: Forward elevator pressure to lower the nose
Coordinated aileron and rudder to level the wings
Reduce power so the speed cannot build
Add power, in proportion to the observed deceleration
quiz.why: Nose-high: increase power in proportion to the observed deceleration, then forward elevator, then coordinated aileron and rudder, almost simultaneously but in that order [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]. Reducing power is the first nose-low step [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

quiz.q: Partial panel, nose-low recovery under way. What tells the learner the airplane is passing through level pitch?
options: The airspeed and altimeter needles stop and reverse
The turn coordinator's miniature aircraft is level
The ball of the inclinometer returns to center
The airspeed needle settles back at normal cruise speed
quiz.why: As the altimeter and airspeed needles slow, the attitude is approaching level; when they stop and reverse, the airplane is passing through level flight [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. The turn coordinator and ball show bank and coordination, not pitch [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

quiz.q: Why does the IFH want a learner in initial training to recover from a nose-low attitude "by the numbers"?
options: Blending the controls overstresses a training airplane
So the recovery is positive and confident, in the right order
The POH/AFM of every trainer requires that sequence
It gives the attitude indicator time to re-erect
quiz.why: All controls change simultaneously in a smooth, proficient recovery, but in initial training a positive, confident recovery should be made by the numbers in the given sequence [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

quiz.q: Your school's older trainer has a spillable attitude indicator. What should your learner believe about it in an unusual attitude?
options: It is accurate to within 5° in any attitude
It is the best instrument to use in extreme attitudes
Its limits may have been exceeded, so don't depend on it
It re-erects itself within seconds of the setup
quiz.why: Do not depend on a spillable attitude indicator, because its upset limits may have been exceeded or it may have failed. The 5° figure is the possible error of a working nonspillable type [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]. Older units tumble past about 60° of pitch or 100° of roll [[23:114|IFH 5-19]].

quiz.q: On the IFH example PFD, what do the red chevrons that appear approaching 30° nose-up show the learner?
options: That the AHRS has failed and attitude is lost
Where the airspeed will be in 6 seconds
The way back to the horizon line, toward level
The stall angle of attack for the current weight
quiz.why: In a nose-high unusual attitude the protection shows red chevrons that point back to the horizon line; they appear approaching 30° nose-up [[23:216|IFH 7-55]] [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]. With an AHRS failure, all protection is lost instead [[23:217|IFH 7-56]].

quiz.q: In a steep nose-low attitude on a PFD, your learner tries to level the boundary between the blue and brown. What does the IFH say?
options: Fine; the color break is the artificial horizon
The break is the horizon only when chevrons show
Either one works once the display has decluttered
The white line is the horizon, not the break
quiz.why: The white line on the attitude indicator is the horizon line. The break between the blue and brown is only a reference and should not be thought of as the artificial horizon [[23:216|IFH 7-55]].

quiz.q: At "recover," your learner pushes forward although the airspeed is already above cruise and rising. Which PTS common error is this mainly?
options: Failure to keep the airplane trimmed for level flight
Incorrect interpretation of the flight instruments
A disorganized flight deck during the setup
Failure to disconnect the autopilot first
quiz.why: Rising airspeed shows a nose-low attitude [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. Pushing means the learner misread the attitude, which the AFH calls incorrect assessment of the upset [[24:112|AFH 5-7]]. The push is a control input, but its cause is the reading.

quiz.q: You hand the airplane to your learner at "recover." Per the AIH, what completes the exchange?
options: The learner nods, since talking adds workload
Your three-step call and reply, then a visual check
The learner's hands on the yoke, with no words needed
You let go as soon as the learner's hands touch it
quiz.why: You say "You have the flight controls," the learner answers "I have the flight controls," and you repeat it; a visual check confirms the other person actually has the controls [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

quiz.q: During a recovery your learner freezes and grips the yoke as the airspeed builds. What does the AIH advise?
options: Talk the learner through it, both of you on the yoke
Wait until the learner lets go before you touch it
Pull the power to idle and let the learner finish
Take the controls, calmly saying you have them
quiz.why: When necessary, take the controls and calmly announce "I have the flight controls." Anxious learners can be incredibly strong, and nothing is gained by fighting for control [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

quiz.q: Which of these is an IFH disorientation demonstration you can give before unusual attitude training?
options: Eyes closed, a slow, coordinated 50° turn felt as a climb
Eyes closed, a spin entry so the learner feels the rotation
A full stall at low altitude so the warning horn is heard
Head down, a 90° bank so the learner feels the high G
quiz.why: With the learner's eyes closed, a slowly entered, well-coordinated turn of about 50° for 90° usually feels like a climb [[23:75|IFH 3-8]]. None of the demonstrations may be flown at low altitudes [[23:75|IFH 3-8]].

quiz.q: Per the AFH, who should be aboard when a pilot practices recovery from unusual attitudes at night?
options: Any private pilot acting as safety pilot
An instrument-rated pilot in the back seat
A flight instructor
A pilot current in night landings
quiz.why: In its section on night flight training, the AFH says practicing recovery from unusual attitudes should only be done with a flight instructor [[24:224|AFH 11-7]].

final_quiz.q: Hand flying in IMC, your learner holds back pressure while reaching behind the seat for a dropped chart. Which IFH causes of unusual attitudes is he setting up?
options: Preoccupation with flight deck duties and poor trim
Turbulence and a mechanical malfunction
Instrument failure and an interpretation error
Wake turbulence and a malfunctioning autopilot system
final_quiz.why: Preoccupation with flight deck duties is on the IFH list [[23:187|IFH 7-26]], and a flight deck interruption while holding pressures can easily lead to an unusual attitude [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. A dropped item should be picked up with minimal head movement because of the Coriolis illusion [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

final_quiz.q: Which illusion is most likely when that learner turns his head to pick up the chart during a prolonged turn?
options: Elevator illusion
Coriolis illusion
Inversion illusion
Autokinesis
final_quiz.why: In a prolonged turn, a head movement in a different plane can set the fluid moving and create the illusion of turning or accelerating on a different axis: the Coriolis illusion [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

final_quiz.q: In the AFH spiral dive recovery, what comes between power to idle and rolling wings level?
options: Full back elevator to stop the descent quickly
Climb power to start regaining the lost altitude
Some forward elevator to unload to about +1 G
Full flaps to keep the airspeed from rising
final_quiz.why: Step 2 is some forward elevator to return to about +1 G before rolling level, which reduces the AOA and G-load and prevents a rolling pullout [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. Adding power is a listed spiral recovery error [[24:132|AFH 5-27]].

final_quiz.q: The attitude indicator shows a 20° left bank, but the turn coordinator is level and the VSI reads zero. What should your learner do first?
options: Roll right until the attitude indicator is level
Reset the heading indicator to the magnetic compass first
Climb above the clouds before troubleshooting
Treat it as a failure; fly the instruments that agree
final_quiz.why: An inconsistency between the attitude indicator and the performance instruments usually means a failure; compare it with the rate-of-turn indicator and VSI, then use the remaining instruments [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]. Following a failed gyro can turn a benign failure into a hazardous one [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].

final_quiz.q: After an AHRS failure in the IFH example glass airplane, which autopilot modes are still available?
options: Roll and altitude hold
Heading and navigation
Vertical speed and approach
No modes at all
final_quiz.why: The AHRS failure removes all autopilot modes except roll and altitude hold [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]. With the air data computer also failed, the manufacturer recommends the roll mode, a wing leveler [[23:219|IFH 7-58]].

final_quiz.q: With both the AHRS and the air data computer failed in the IFH example airplane, which instruments are left?
options: A standby turn coordinator, altimeter and compass
Standby airspeed, attitude indicator, altimeter, compass
The PFD attitude display plus the standby altimeter and VSI
Only the magnetic compass and the GPS moving map
final_quiz.why: Only the standby instruments remain: an analog airspeed indicator, attitude indicator, altimeter and magnetic compass. There is no standby turn coordinator [[23:219|IFH 7-58]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner levels the wings in a nose-low recovery with the ball well out of center. What does the IFH warn?
options: The attitude indicator tumbles past its roll limit
The airspeed indicator reads high in any skid
Slip and skid sensations can aggravate disorientation
The VSI reverses and shows a false climb
final_quiz.why: The ball should be centered. If it is not, skidding and slipping sensations can easily aggravate disorientation and retard the recovery [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

final_quiz.q: Which telling-and-doing step lets you check a learner's grasp of the recovery sequence before the learner has to fly it?
options: Instructor tells, instructor does
Learner tells, learner does
Learner does, instructor evaluates
Learner tells, instructor does
final_quiz.why: In "learner tells, instructor does" the learner tells you what to do while you fly, so you can evaluate understanding and correct a misunderstanding before the learner is absorbed in controlling the airplane [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

final_quiz.q: As your learner, the examiner recovers well but then stays 300 feet below the assigned altitude. What does the IFH say?
options: Return to the original altitude after stabilizing
Stay at the new altitude, since the recovery is complete
Climb back at the steepest rate the airplane can give
Hold the new altitude until ATC assigns a new one
final_quiz.why: If the unusual attitude began at an altitude assigned by an instructor or ATC, return to it after stabilizing in straight-and-level flight [[23:189|IFH 7-28]], at about double the deviation and never more than the optimum rate [[23:197|IFH 7-36]] [[23:198|IFH 7-37]].

final_quiz.q: Why does the AFH say eyes-closed unusual attitude training differs from a real upset?
options: Eyes closed makes recovery harder than in real life
Eyes closed takes away the element of surprise
Eyes closed is not allowed in normal category airplanes
Eyes closed hides the instruments needed to recover
final_quiz.why: An upset centers on unintentional situations that may cause startle; in unusual attitude training the pilot is often told to close their eyes, and any element of surprise disappears [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]. Realistic distractions in scenario training add it back [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner reads bank direction from the pointer on the bank scale and rolls the wrong way. What does the PHAK advise?
options: Use the pointer, since it always moves with the bank
Use the heading indicator, since the scale is unreliable
Reset the miniature aircraft with the adjustment knob
Scale for amount; miniature aircraft for direction
final_quiz.why: Some bank scales move opposite to the actual bank, which may confuse the pilot. Use the scale only to control the degree of bank, and the miniature aircraft against the horizon bar for its direction [[1:221|PHAK 8-19]].

final_quiz.q: On partial panel, what may your learner read from the turn coordinator during the recovery?
options: Rate and direction of turn, not the bank angle
The exact bank angle, like a roll scale
Pitch as well as bank while the airplane rolls
Nothing, since it fails with the vacuum system
final_quiz.why: The turn coordinator indicates only the rate and direction of turn; it does not display a specific angle of bank [[1:219|PHAK 8-17]]. Its canted gyro senses roll and yaw [[23:116|IFH 5-21]], and it does not sense pitch [[23:117|IFH 5-22]].

final_quiz.q: Which AFH idea describes control and power inputs matched to the size and rate of an unintended excursion?
options: Full deflection opposite to the upset
Proportional counter-response
Equal inputs on all three axes
Power reduced by altitude lost
final_quiz.why: Proportional counter-response is the timely use of flight controls and thrust to manage an unintended attitude or envelope excursion [[24:111|AFH 5-6]]; inputs should be in direct proportion to the amount and rate of change, to avoid overstressing the airplane [[24:109|AFH 5-4]].

final_quiz.q: In the PFD trainer your learner is past 60° of bank and unsure which way to roll. What does the display give him?
options: Red chevrons that point toward the wing to raise first
A slip/skid indicator that turns red
A roll index line showing the shortest way to wings level
An aural callout of the bank angle
final_quiz.why: When bank increases beyond 60°, the roll index continues as a line that shows the shortest direction to roll the wings level [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]. The chevrons are for pitch [[23:217|IFH 7-56]].

final_quiz.q: The IFH lists "failure to practice basic instrument skills" as an unusual attitude error. Why does it matter for recoveries?
options: Basic skills are not tested on the instrument checkride
Recoveries use different control inputs than basics
The attitude indicator is not used in basic maneuvers
Every basic instrument error is aggravated in a recovery
final_quiz.why: All of the errors of basic instrument skills are aggravated during unusual attitude recoveries until the elementary skills have been mastered [[23:190|IFH 7-29]].

takeaways: Task H is on every CFII checkride, demonstrated under a view-limiting device.
Teach the eight IFH conditions by name, each with a prevention habit; disorientation and instrument failure matter most in IMC.
Read before you move: airspeed tells nose-high or nose-low, the turn coordinator and ball tell the bank.
Nose-high: power up, push, roll. Nose-low: power back, roll, then smooth back pressure.
Partial panel: level pitch is when the airspeed and altimeter needles stop and reverse; on glass, know what an AHRS failure takes away.
Set up with eyes closed and a three-step exchange, keep your eyes outside, then "recover, you have the flight controls."
Explain as you fly, in the briefed order; for errors, name it, explain the cause, give the fix.
cfi_notes: Nose-high: the IFH order is power, pitch, bank [[23:188|IFH 7-27]], while the AFH stall recovery is angle of attack, roll, power [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Teach that the stall warning or buffet decides: stalled means the stall recovery, otherwise the IFH nose-high sequence.

Nose-low: the IFH order is power, bank, pitch [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]; the AFH spiral procedure adds an unload to about +1 G before rolling [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. They do not conflict; the unload matters in a steep, high-G spiral.

The sources give two return-to-altitude limits: double the deviation but never more than the optimum rate of 500 to 1,000 fpm [[23:197|IFH 7-36]] [[23:198|IFH 7-37]], and twice the deviation not to exceed 500 fpm in the glass straight-and-level section [[23:155|IFH 6-22]]. Tell the learner which one you use.

Attitude indicator limits differ: about 60° pitch and 100° roll for older units [[23:114|IFH 5-19]], or 60° to 70° pitch and 100° to 110° bank, with some ±25° pitch displays that peg or tumble [[1:221|PHAK 8-19]]. Know the instrument in your airplane.

How it is tested: Task H on every test, with you under a view-limiting device and often after the scenario; the PTS asks for full panel and partial panel or backup instruments, and the examiner acts as your learner for S2 without simulating anything unsafe (FAA-S-8081-9E).
The PTS Task lists FAA-H-8083-9, FAA-H-8083-15 and FAA-S-ACS-8 without edition letters; this lesson uses the current AIH (FAA-H-8083-9B) and IFH (FAA-H-8083-15B).

The IFH glass numbers (chevrons, declutter angles, no standby turn coordinator, autopilot roll mode) come from the system in its figures [[23:217|IFH 7-56]] [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]. Check the AFM or supplement for the airplane you will test in.

Eyes-closed setups remove surprise [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]. Once they are solid, let an attitude develop during a realistic distraction such as a chart task or resetting the clock [[25:180|AIH 9-10]], because scenario training with realistic distractions prepares a pilot for startle [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

Turn needle airplanes: the PTS footnote substitutes the turn needle for the turn coordinator's miniature aircraft. The turn-and-slip gyro responds to yaw, while the turn coordinator senses roll and yaw and first shows the rate of roll [[23:116|IFH 5-21]].
gaps: No source gives a minimum altitude for unusual attitude practice; the AFH asks for enough altitude for a recovery and recommends stall practice that recovers no lower than 1,500 feet AGL in single-engine airplanes [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

No FAA source here gives a step-by-step setup script (eyes closed, head down, hands off, then "recover"). The setup in this lesson is built from the AFH note on eyes-closed training [[24:107|AFH 5-2]], the IFH disorientation demonstrations [[23:75|IFH 3-8]] and the AIH exchange of controls [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].
No source here says how to simulate an AHRS failure in flight; the IFH says only "simulated or rendered inoperative" [[23:194|IFH 7-33]]. Use the AFM and your school's procedures.
The PTS gives no numeric tolerances for this Task; the sources describe sequence and technique only.
Airplane-specific recovery procedures, power settings and configuration items come from the POH/AFM, which is not among these sources.
The AFH upset recovery template (Figure 5-3) and spiral dive template (Figure 5-18) are graphics whose content is not in the handbook text [[24:111|AFH 5-6]] [[24:132|AFH 5-27]].

activities.title: Numbers behind a gentle recovery
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: After a recovery your learner is level 300 feet below the assigned altitude. Using the IFH 7-36 rule of thumb (double the deviation, never more than the airplane's optimum rate, here 800 fpm), what vertical speed should he use to return?
items.why: Double the deviation: 2 x 300 = 600 fpm, below the 800 fpm optimum rate; the IFH says an optimum rate varies between 500 and 1,000 fpm [[23:197|IFH 7-36]] [[23:198|IFH 7-37]]. The IFH glass straight-and-level section caps the same rule at 500 fpm [[23:155|IFH 6-22]], so tell the learner which rule you use.

items.q: At 600 fpm, how many seconds does that 300-foot climb take once the rate is set?
items.why: 300 / 600 = 0.5 minute = 30 seconds, using the double-the-deviation rate [[23:197|IFH 7-36]].

items.q: A trainer with a normal stall speed of 50 knots is pulled to 4 G in a hurried pullout. Using the PHAK square-root rule, at what speed can it stall?
items.why: The square root of 4 is 2, and 50 x 2 = 100 knots [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]] [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].

items.q: An older airplane stalls at 60 knots. Using the PHAK approximation, about what is its design maneuvering speed?
items.why: About 1.7 times the normal stalling speed: 60 x 1.7 = 102 knots. Even below VA, full inputs in more than one axis at once are not protected [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].

activities.title: True or false: setup, safety and the exchange
activities.intro: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

cards.s: On the CFII practical test the examiner may simulate any learner error, even one that could damage the airplane, to see if you catch it.
cards.why: False. The evaluator will not simulate any condition that may jeopardize safe flight or result in possible damage to the aircraft (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction).

cards.s: When handing the controls back to you, the learner keeps flying until you say "I have the flight controls."
The 60° bank and 30° pitch parachute limits of 14 CFR 91.307(c) apply during a flight test for a certificate or rating.
cards.why: False. Paragraph (c) does not apply to flight tests for pilot certification or rating [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(d)]].

cards.s: Disorientation demonstrations are fine at low altitude as long as an instructor is aboard.
cards.why: False. They should not be attempted at low altitudes or without an instructor or appropriate safety pilot [[23:75|IFH 3-8]].

cards.s: Having the learner close their eyes during the setup removes the element of surprise.
cards.why: True [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]. Add realistic distractions later to train for startle [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

cards.s: The PTS has you use a view-limiting device when you demonstrate this Task.
cards.why: True. The PTS names Area VI, Task H as one where the applicant uses a view-limiting device (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction).

activities.title: A partial panel lesson, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are teaching an instrument learner in a six-pack trainer. The attitude and heading indicators are covered, the weather is good VMC, the area is clear, and you are the safety pilot.

steps.s: Before the setup, the learner is flying. You want the airplane.
options: Grab the yoke and start maneuvering, since the plan was briefed
Use the three-step exchange and check that the learner let go
Tell the learner to let go and count to three before you take it
Have the learner keep a light touch on the yoke as you maneuver
steps.why: The learner gives control with the same three steps you use, and a visual check confirms who has it [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

steps.s: Eyes closed, you fly a slow climbing turn right, then a descending turn left. You stop with the airspeed rising and 30° of left bank and say "Recover, you have the flight controls." What should the learner do?
options: Pull back first to stop the descent, then level the wings
Power back, level the wings on the turn coordinator, then raise the nose
Add power to hold altitude while rolling the wings level
Wait for you to uncover the attitude indicator
steps.why: Nose-low: reduce power, correct the bank with coordinated aileron and rudder by the turn coordinator, then raise the nose with smooth back pressure [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

steps.s: During the pull the needles slow, stop and start to reverse. The learner keeps pulling.
options: Say nothing; the VSI will show him the climb
Take the controls at once and end the lesson
Tell him he is passing level and to ease off now
Tell him to add power to stop the climb
steps.why: When the needles stop and reverse, the airplane is passing through level flight; keep a fast cross-check for overcontrolling [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

steps.s: Next setup: nose-high, airspeed low and falling. The learner adds power and pushes until the airspeed is far past cruise.
options: Name it: too much push; stop when the needles reverse
Praise it: a dive is the surest way to avoid a stall
Tell him to add even more power to recover faster
Uncover the attitude indicator so he can see the dive
steps.why: Forward pressure is only to lower the nose and prevent a stall; level pitch shows when the airspeed and altimeter needles reverse and stabilize [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

steps.s: In the debrief he says he is now ready for a real vacuum failure in cloud.
options: Agree; two good recoveries prove the skill is set
Explain the skill is perishable and needs regular practice
Tell him partial panel will not be needed in his flying
Tell him to rely on the autopilot in any failure
steps.why: Upset recovery skills are perishable and need continuous reinforcement [[24:110|AFH 5-5]]; pilots should avoid IMC when not proficient [[23:221|IFH 7-60]].
